stimulus.text:
| Society | Environment | Main way of getting food | Settlement |
| Pueblo peoples | Arid Southwest | Dry farming of maize, beans, and squash | Permanent adobe villages |
| Iroquois villagers | Northeast woodlands | Three sisters farming, with hunting and fishing | Permanent villages |
| Chinook peoples | Rainy Pacific coast | Fishing, hunting, and foraging | Permanent villages with marked social ranks |
| Great Plains peoples | Grasslands | Bison hunting on foot, with some farming in river valleys | Mobile camps for much of the year |
| Great Basin peoples | Arid basin between mountain ranges | Hunting and gathering, moving with the seasons | Mobile camps |
stimulus.source_note: Table compiled from the grounding books; see grounding.

source: original; converted from original-u1-native-06; distractor B rewritten against the grounding books
stem: Historians observe that where maize farming supported dense populations, complex hierarchies developed, while societies without intensive farming stayed smaller and more mobile. Which explanation best accounts for this pattern?

options.text: Farming societies owned superior weapons that forced neighboring peoples to obey them.
options.misconception: Explains hierarchy with weapons, but the pattern is about food production.

options.text: Mobile societies had no leaders at all, since moving too often made leadership impossible.
options.misconception: Turns smaller mobile life into a claim that mobile peoples had no leaders at all.

options.text: Maize could only be planted by societies that already had kings and priests.
options.misconception: Reverses the causation: farming came first and made hierarchy possible.

options.text: Farming produced food surpluses that fed non-farming specialists like chiefs and priests.

rationales.A: The pattern is about food production, not about weapons forcing neighbors to obey.
rationales.B: Mobile peoples did have leaders; small, mobile life follows from limited food, not from having no leaders at all.
rationales.C: Farming came first and made hierarchy possible, so kings and priests cannot be the cause of planting.
rationales.D: A surplus is the key: extra food supports full-time leaders, religious specialists, and builders.
rationales.general:
1. Name the pattern. Where maize farming fed dense peoples, hierarchies grew, and where it did not, life stayed smaller and mobile.
2. Ask what farming adds. It adds a surplus, food beyond what farming families need.
3. Ask what a surplus buys. It pays the salaries of people who do not farm: chiefs, priests, and builders eat from the extra.
4. Follow the chain. Surplus feeds specialists, and specialists make hierarchy.
Remember: to explain hierarchy, follow the surplus, not the weapons.
